\chapter{Tastes}
\label{ch:te-tastes}
\hlchaptermodality{73}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the tastes of a Telugu meal and take my leave when it is finished.}

Complete TE-C73-astringent and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[tīpi]{\te{తీపి} (tīpi) — sweet, sweetness}

\label{lesson:TE-C73-sweet}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bēraṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తీపి}}
\textbf{\te{తీపి}} (\emph{tīpi}) — \textquotedblleft{}sweet, sweetness\textquotedblright{}.

\te{తీపి} is sweetness — the taste, and the quality of anything that has it.

It is inherited. \te{చక్కెర} gives it in a kitchen and a \te{పండు} gives it on a \te{చెట్టు}, and a person described as \te{తీపి} is being called good company.

Telugu counts its tastes rather than gesturing at them, and \te{తీపి} is the one every count opens with.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One. The taste every count opens with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tīpi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tīpi}, then \emph{cakkera}, and say which one is the taste
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{తీపి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sweet, sweetness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pulupu]{\te{పులుపు} (pulupu) — sour, sourness}

\label{lesson:TE-C73-sour}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tīpi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పులుపు}}
\textbf{\te{పులుపు}} (\emph{pulupu}) — \textquotedblleft{}sour, sourness\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పులుపు} is sourness — tamarind, lime, \te{పెరుగు} left a day too long.

It is inherited and it is not a complaint. A Telugu meal wants \te{పులుపు} in it on purpose; the everyday tamarind stew is built around exactly this taste.

Said of a face it means what it means in English, and it is said most often of children who have just been told no.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: \te{తీపి} and \te{పులుపు}, and a meal wants both of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pulupu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tīpi}, then \emph{pulupu}, and say which one is in curd
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పులుపు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sour, sourness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cēdu]{\te{చేదు} (cēdu) — bitter, bitterness}

\label{lesson:TE-C73-bitter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pulupu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చేదు}}
\textbf{\te{చేదు}} (\emph{cēdu}) — \textquotedblleft{}bitter, bitterness\textquotedblright{}.

\te{చేదు} is bitterness — neem leaf, some greens, most medicine.

It is inherited, and Telugu does not treat it as a fault. Bitter is eaten deliberately at the opening of the year and at the opening of a meal, on the understanding that it does you good.

It carries over into speech unchanged. \te{చేదు} news is bad news, and a \te{చేదు} truth is one you are told anyway.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. The one eaten on purpose.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cēdu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cēdu}, then \emph{tīpi}, and say which one is eaten first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చేదు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}bitter, bitterness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāraṁ]{\te{కారం} (kāraṁ) — pungency, heat}

\label{lesson:TE-C73-pungent}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cēdu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కారం}}
\textbf{\te{కారం}} (\emph{kāraṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}pungency, heat\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కారం} is heat — the bite of \te{మిరప}, and by an easy extension the chilli powder itself.

Ask for something with \te{తక్కువ} \te{కారం} and you will be understood anywhere, though in one or two households you will be heard as having said something mildly insulting.

It is inherited. Do not read it into the end of \te{నమస్కారం}, which is a different word altogether, Sanskrit, and means a making.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. And the one you may want \te{తక్కువ} of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kāraṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kāraṁ}, then \emph{takkuva} and \emph{kāraṁ} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కారం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}pungency, heat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vagaru]{\te{వగరు} (vagaru) — astringent}

\label{lesson:TE-C73-astringent}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kāraṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వగరు}}
\textbf{\te{వగరు}} (\emph{vagaru}) — \textquotedblleft{}astringent\textquotedblright{}.

\te{వగరు} is astringency — the dry, puckering taste of an unripe \te{పండు}, of raw banana, of \te{టీ} left to stand.

English has no everyday word for it and Telugu has had one for as long as it has been written down. Once you can name it you begin noticing it, which is most of what a word is for.

With \te{ఉప్పు}, which you already have, that is the full set a Telugu cook thinks in: \te{తీపి}, \te{పులుపు}, \te{చేదు}, \te{కారం}, \te{వగరు} and salt. A meal carrying all of them is finished, and so is the visit — \te{వెళ్ళొస్తాను}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{తీపి}, \te{పులుపు}, \te{చేదు}, \te{కారం}, \te{వగరు}. The tastes a Telugu meal is built from, and the last of them names what nothing else does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vagaru}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then take your leave with \emph{veḷḷostānu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{వగరు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}astringent\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
